Viết Task 1 mô tả quy trình thủ công theo đúng trình tự, không thêm ý kiến

exam_strategy: Bài tổng hợp nhiều dạng: làm dạng cần đọc toàn bài (headings, global) trước hoặc sau cùng một cách nhất quán; câu hỏi thái độ dựa vào tính từ/trạng từ đánh giá của người viết.

grammar.title: Advanced concession and contrast
grammar.explanation_vi: Ở band 7, nhượng bộ không chỉ dùng although: while/whilst (trong khi, dù), much as + mệnh đề (dù rất…), admittedly (phải thừa nhận), nevertheless/nonetheless (tuy vậy – đứng đầu câu sau). Cấu trúc Adjective + as/though + S + be (Popular as the festival is, …) trang trọng, rất hợp Task 2.
grammar.form: While / Whilst + mệnh đề, … · Much as + S + V, … · Admittedly, … However/Nevertheless, … · Adj + as + S + be, … · despite / in spite of + N/V-ing
examples: While tourism brings income, it can also turn rituals into performances.
Much as I admire traditional crafts, I accept that they must adapt to survive.
Popular as the festival is, many residents feel excluded from it.
examples_vi: Dù du lịch mang lại thu nhập, nó cũng có thể biến nghi lễ thành màn trình diễn.
Dù tôi rất ngưỡng mộ nghề thủ công truyền thống, tôi chấp nhận rằng chúng phải thay đổi để tồn tại.
Lễ hội nổi tiếng là vậy, nhiều cư dân vẫn cảm thấy bị gạt ra ngoài.
grammar.trap: Much as + mệnh đề (không dùng với danh từ). Cấu trúc “Adj + as + S + be” không có “as” ở đầu (sai: “As popular as the festival is, …” khi muốn nghĩa nhượng bộ). Nevertheless đứng đầu câu mới, có dấu phẩy, không nối hai mệnh đề bằng dấu phẩy đơn.
items: ___ tourism creates jobs, it can damage local traditions. (While / Despite)
While
While + mệnh đề = dù/trong khi.
___ as I enjoy festivals, I find them too crowded. (một từ)
Much
Much as + mệnh đề = dù rất…
The craft is declining. ___, young designers are reviving it. (Nevertheless / Although)
Nevertheless
Đầu câu mới, có dấu phẩy → Nevertheless.
Rewrite: Although the festival is popular, … → Popular ___ the festival is, …
as
Adj + as + S + be = nhượng bộ.
___ the high cost, the museum remains free for children. (Despite / Although)
Despite
Despite + cụm danh từ.
___, the policy has had some success. However, its benefits are uneven. (từ thừa nhận)
Admittedly
Admittedly = phải thừa nhận rằng.
In spite ___ the rain, the parade went ahead.
of
in spite of + danh từ.
Correct the error: Much as the festival, I prefer quieter celebrations.
Much as I enjoy the festival, I prefer quieter celebrations.
Much as + mệnh đề đầy đủ.

readings.title: Who owns a culture?
readings.strategy: Bài tổng hợp: làm headings trước để nắm cấu trúc; YES/NO/NOT GIVEN dựa vào câu có quan điểm người viết; multiple choice thái độ đọc kỹ tính từ đánh giá.
readings.instruction_vi: Bài đọc khoảng 880 từ, 13 câu: 4 câu headings, 5 câu YES/NO/NOT GIVEN và 4 câu multiple choice về thái độ và ý chính.
headings: i. Borrowing as a long-standing human practice
iv. The difficulty of defining a single owner
v. A ban on all foreign influence
vi. The economics of craft exports
paragraphs: A

In recent years, debates about cultural appropriation – the adoption of elements of one culture by members of another – have become increasingly common, particularly in fashion, music and food. A designer uses a traditional pattern from an indigenous community; a pop star adopts a hairstyle associated with a minority group; a restaurant chain sells a sacred dish as a party snack. Critics describe such cases as theft or disrespect, while defenders reply that cultures have always borrowed from one another and that cultural exchange enriches everyone. Both positions, in my view, contain important truths, and the difficulty lies in telling one kind of borrowing from another.
B

There is no doubt that cultures have always developed through contact with others. Musical instruments, cooking techniques, religious ideas and styles of clothing have travelled along trade routes for thousands of years, often changing as they moved. Many of the traditions that communities now regard as most authentically their own were originally adopted from elsewhere. A world in which every culture kept strictly to its own practices would not only be impossible to achieve; it would be considerably poorer. Even practices that seem deeply rooted in one place, such as particular dishes or forms of dress, often turn out on closer inspection to combine ingredients, techniques or ideas that arrived from far away, sometimes centuries ago.
C

The problem arises when exchange takes place between groups of very unequal power. When a large company profits from designs created by a small community, without permission, credit or payment, the relationship looks less like exchange and more like extraction. The community may also see its practices presented inaccurately, stripped of their meaning or associated with stereotypes. In such cases, I would argue, the objection is not to borrowing as such, but to the unfair terms on which it occurs.
D

Defining ownership, however, is far from straightforward. Cultures are not fixed, and members of the same community often disagree about which practices are sacred, which can be shared and who has the right to decide. A traditional textile pattern may be used by dozens of villages, none of which can claim to have invented it. Legal systems designed to protect individual inventions are poorly suited to protecting knowledge that has been developed collectively over generations.
E

Some communities have responded by developing their own rules. In the fictional mountain region of Tessaly, weavers' associations have created a certification label that identifies textiles made by local artisans using traditional methods. Designers who wish to use traditional patterns can apply for permission and agree to share profits with the association. The scheme is voluntary, and some outside designers ignore it, but it has given the weavers a stronger position in negotiations and helped consumers identify authentic products.
F

Representation is another concern. When museums, films or advertisements portray a culture, the people of that culture have often had little say in how they are shown. Increasingly, cultural institutions are inviting communities to take part in deciding how their objects and stories are presented. This ethical representation can be slower and more complicated, but it tends to produce displays that are both more accurate and more respectful. In some cases, communities have also asked for objects to be returned, or for decisions about display to be shared formally between institutions and community representatives.
G

It would be a mistake, though, to treat every use of another culture's elements as suspicious. Much of what is described as appropriation is in fact appreciation – people learning a language, cooking unfamiliar dishes or studying traditional music with genuine respect and curiosity. Discouraging such interest could reduce intercultural dialogue at precisely the moment when it is most needed.
H

A useful set of questions may help to distinguish between the two. Who benefits from the use? Was permission sought where appropriate? Is the practice presented accurately and with credit? Is something sacred being treated as a commercial product? These questions will not settle every case, but they shift the debate away from simple accusations and towards the conditions that make cultural exchange fair.
I

Ultimately, the question of who owns a culture may be less useful than the question of who has a voice in how it is shared. Where communities have real control over their heritage – through associations, agreements or participation in institutions – exchange is more likely to be welcomed than resented. Seen in this way, the debate is not about building walls around cultures, but about ensuring that the people whose heritage is involved are partners rather than bystanders when it travels.

readings.title: Saving a minority language
readings.strategy: TFNG + short answer: chú ý số liệu và các mốc thời gian; phân biệt mong muốn của cộng đồng với kết quả đã đạt được.
paragraphs: A

Linguists estimate that around half of the world's roughly seven thousand languages may no longer be spoken by the end of this century. When a language disappears, communities lose not only a means of communication but also songs, stories and knowledge about local plants, animals and landscapes that may never have been written down. The decline of a minority language usually happens gradually, as parents decide that their children will have better opportunities if they speak the dominant language of the country.
B

The fictional island community of Kerran offers an example of how this process can be slowed. Fifty years ago, the Kerranese language was spoken by most adults on the island but by very few children. Schools taught only in the national language, and many parents believed that speaking Kerranese at home would hold their children back.
C

The turning point came when a group of parents opened a small nursery in which all activities took place in Kerranese. The nursery was popular, and within a decade the island had several primary schools teaching mainly in the local language, with the national language introduced gradually. Research comparing children from these schools with those from national-language schools found no disadvantage in their later exam results, and some advantages in reading.
D

Technology has also played a part. Volunteers have recorded thousands of hours of older speakers telling stories and describing traditional work, creating an archive that is used in schools. A Kerranese keyboard for mobile phones, released several years ago, has been downloaded by a significant proportion of the island's young people, who now use the language in text messages and on social media.
E

Not everything has gone smoothly. Some older speakers feel that the Kerranese taught in schools is simplified and that younger speakers mix it with words from the national language. Linguists, however, point out that all living languages change and that mixing is a sign of a language being used, not of its decline.
F

Today, the number of children who speak Kerranese has risen steadily for twenty years, although it remains lower than it was a century ago. The community's experience suggests that intergenerational transmission – passing a language from parents to children – is the key to survival, and that schools and technology work best when they support families rather than replace them.
G

Other minority-language communities have begun to visit Kerran to learn from its experience. Organisers there emphasise that no single measure was decisive. Nurseries, schools, recordings and mobile technology each played a part, but none would have worked without parents who chose, every day, to speak the language at home.

readings.title: Festivals and the visitor economy
readings.strategy: Multiple choice về ý chính và thái độ: phương án quá tuyệt đối (always, never) thường sai với bài thận trọng.
paragraphs: A

Traditional festivals are increasingly marketed to international visitors. Regional governments promote them in tourism campaigns, travel companies sell festival packages, and images of colourful parades and lantern processions are shared widely online. For many communities, the income from visitors has made it possible to maintain traditions that might otherwise have faded.
B

Yet the growth of festival tourism raises difficult questions. When a ceremony that once took place for the community becomes a performance for paying spectators, its meaning can change. Some participants report that they now feel like actors rather than worshippers, and that the timing and form of ceremonies are adjusted to suit tour schedules.
C

Commodification – turning cultural practices into products for sale – is not always harmful. Selling crafts, food and performances can give younger people a reason to learn traditional skills, and the income can support the elders who teach them. The problem arises when commercial pressures begin to dictate what is preserved and what is abandoned, so that only the most photogenic elements survive.
D

Several communities have tried to find a balance. In some places, the most sacred parts of a festival are held privately, while public events designed for visitors take place separately. Elsewhere, community-led initiatives decide how many tourists can attend and how income is shared. Researchers studying these arrangements suggest that festivals managed by local residents tend to retain their meaning better than those organised mainly by outside companies.
E

Visitors themselves can make a difference. Learning about the significance of a ceremony before attending, following local guidance about photography and spending money in locally owned businesses all help to ensure that tourism supports rather than undermines the communities involved. Choosing smaller, locally run tours instead of large packages can also spread income more widely within a community.
F

Festival tourism, then, is neither simply a threat nor simply a benefit. Its effects depend largely on who controls it. Where communities retain cultural agency – the power to make decisions about their own traditions – tourism can strengthen heritage rather than weaken it.
G

For policy makers, the lesson is that promoting a festival internationally should go hand in hand with supporting the people who keep it alive. Funding for elders who teach traditional skills, rules that limit visitor numbers at sensitive ceremonies and transparent agreements about how income is shared can all help ensure that a festival's growing fame does not come at the expense of its meaning. Without such measures, a community may find that the attention it once welcomed has gradually taken control of the tradition itself.

listenings.title: Booking a place on a cultural tour
listenings.strategy: Note completion: chú ý tên địa danh được đánh vần, giá và những thay đổi lịch trình.
listenings.pre_listening: Trước khi nghe: đọc ghi chú, đoán chỗ cần số, ngày hay tên riêng.
listenings.trap: Lịch trình hoặc giá thường được nhắc theo phiên bản cũ rồi cập nhật.
listenings.transcript:
Agent: Heritage Trails, good morning. This is Marco.
Caller: Hello, I'm interested in your weekend tour of craft villages in the north.
Agent: Of course. That's our 'Makers of the Valley' tour. It visits three villages over two days. On the first day you'll see a pottery village and a village that makes conical hats, and on the second day a silk-weaving village.
Caller: Lovely. What dates are available?
Agent: The next tours are on the fourteenth and twenty-first of next month. The fourteenth was nearly full, but we've just added a second minibus, so there's space on both.
Caller: The fourteenth would be best. How much is it?
Agent: It's one hundred and eighty-five dollars per person, which includes accommodation in a family guesthouse, all meals and the workshops. It used to include a river cruise as well, but that's been replaced by a cooking class with the guesthouse family.
Caller: That sounds even better. What are the workshops?
Agent: In the pottery village you'll shape a small bowl on a wheel, and at the silk village you'll try the loom. The hats are made from palm leaves, and you'll learn how the leaves are dried and pressed before they're sewn onto a bamboo frame.
Caller: Is there much walking?
Agent: Around five kilometres in total, on flat paths. You'll need comfortable shoes, and a light jacket, as evenings can be cool in the valley.
Caller: Can I take photos everywhere?
Agent: Mostly, yes, but please ask before photographing people, and photography isn't allowed inside the temple at the silk village.
Caller: OK. What's the meeting point?
Agent: The tour leaves at seven a.m. from outside the Opera House. Our guide's name is Linh – L-I-N-H – and she'll be holding a green flag.
Caller: Perfect. Could I book two places, please? The name is Sarah Whitlock.
Agent: Of course. I'll email the confirmation now.

listenings.title: Lecture: how traditions are passed on
listenings.strategy: Sentence completion trong bài giảng: đọc trước câu, nghe từ khóa đồng nghĩa; đáp án thường là danh từ trừu tượng.
listenings.transcript:
Lecturer: Today I'd like to talk about how intangible heritage – practices, knowledge and skills rather than physical objects – is transmitted from one generation to the next, and what happens when that process breaks down.
For most of human history, traditions were passed on informally. Children learned songs, crafts and rituals by watching and helping older relatives. Learning was embedded in daily life rather than separated into lessons. Anthropologists call this situated learning, and it remains the main way many skills are transmitted today.
This informal system depends on certain conditions. Different generations need to live close to one another and spend time together, and the skill needs to have some value in everyday life. When young people move to cities for education or work, or when a craft can no longer earn a living, transmission can stop within a single generation.
Communities and governments have responded in several ways. One is formal training – apprenticeship programmes or courses in which master practitioners teach students. These can be effective, but they sometimes change the tradition itself, because teaching in a classroom requires knowledge to be broken into standard steps that were never fixed before.
A second response is documentation: recording songs, filming craftspeople at work and writing down oral histories. Documentation preserves information, but it does not by itself keep a tradition alive. A recording of a song is not the same as a community that still sings it.
The third response, and in my view the most promising, is to create new contexts in which traditions are useful or meaningful. Festivals, markets for craft products and the use of traditional designs in contemporary fashion can give young people reasons to learn. Critics worry that this leads to commercialisation, and that's a fair concern, but research suggests that traditions which find a new role tend to survive longer than those that are only preserved in archives.
For next week's seminar, please identify one tradition from your own background and analyse which of these three responses would suit it best.

listenings.title: Students prepare a talk on food culture
listenings.strategy: Nghe đề xuất, phản đối và quyết định cuối cùng; câu hỏi thường hỏi lý do của quyết định.
listenings.transcript:
Tutor: So, Anh and Lucas, you're giving a talk on food and cultural identity. How are you planning to approach it?
Anh: We'd like to focus on one dish that has travelled around the world, and look at how it changed in different places.
Lucas: My first idea was pizza, but there's already so much written about it that we thought it would be hard to say anything new.
Anh: So we've chosen pho instead. It's interesting because the version most people outside Vietnam know is quite different from what people eat in Hanoi.
Tutor: In what way?
Anh: Abroad, it's often served with a big plate of herbs, bean sprouts and sauces, which is actually closer to the southern style. In Hanoi, it's usually simpler, and people sometimes see adding lots of sauce as spoiling the broth.
Lucas: We also found that some restaurant chains abroad have created versions that would be unrecognisable in Vietnam – with ingredients like cheese.
Tutor: Are you going to criticise those versions?
Anh: We thought about it, but we decided that would be too simple. Many dishes change when they travel, and Vietnamese food itself includes influences from China and France. So our argument is that change isn't the problem in itself.
Lucas: The problem is more about who gets credit and who benefits. Some of the most successful chains abroad aren't owned by Vietnamese people, and their marketing barely mentions Vietnam.
Tutor: That's a nuanced position. How will you support it?
Anh: We're going to interview the owners of two local restaurants – one run by a Vietnamese family and one by a large company.
Tutor: Good idea. And visuals?
Lucas: We were going to show maps of how the dish spread, but we've decided photographs of the different versions side by side would be more striking.
Tutor: Fine. Keep the talk to fifteen minutes and leave five minutes for questions.

questions.prompt: Why did they reject pizza as a topic?
options: A. It is not popular enough.
B. Too much has already been written about it.
C. Their tutor disliked it.

writing.instruction_vi: Quy trình làm nón lá: overview nêu số bước, điểm bắt đầu và sản phẩm cuối; mô tả theo trình tự bằng bị động và từ nối trình tự, không thêm ý kiến. Viết ít nhất 150 từ (mục tiêu 170–190).
writing.task: The diagram shows the stages in making a traditional conical hat by hand. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features. Write at least 150 words.

rows: Palm leaves are collected and dried in the sun
Leaves are pressed flat with a heated iron and sorted by size
Bamboo is split into thin strips and bent into 16 rings
Rings are fixed onto a cone-shaped wooden mould
Leaves are laid over the frame in two layers
Leaves are sewn onto the rings by hand
The hat is removed, varnished and dried

writing.sample_answer:
The diagram illustrates the stages involved in making a traditional conical hat by hand, from the preparation of raw materials to the finished product.

Overall, the process consists of seven main stages, which can be divided into two phases: preparing the leaves and the frame, and then assembling and finishing the hat. The process relies on natural materials such as palm leaves and bamboo, together with simple hand tools.

At the beginning of the process, young palm leaves are collected and dried in the sun. They are then pressed flat with a heated iron and sorted according to their size. Meanwhile, bamboo is split into thin strips, which are bent to form sixteen rings of different diameters. These rings are subsequently fixed onto a cone-shaped wooden mould, creating the frame of the hat.

Once the frame is ready, the pressed leaves are laid over it in two layers. Next, the leaves are sewn onto the bamboo rings by hand using a needle and nylon thread. Finally, the completed hat is removed from the mould, coated with varnish to protect it from rain and left to dry, after which it is ready for use.

Thân bài 2: lắp ráp và hoàn thiện (once, next, finally).

essay.prompt: Some people believe that globalisation is causing local cultures to lose their identity. Others think it allows cultures to share and enrich one another. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.
planning_prompts: Mở bài: hai quan điểm và ý kiến (cả hai đều đúng một phần; kết quả phụ thuộc quyền kiểm soát).
Thân bài 1: nguy cơ – đồng nhất hóa, ngôn ngữ thiểu số, thương mại hóa.
Thân bài 2: lợi ích – trao đổi, phục hưng truyền thống, thị trường mới.
Ý kiến + kết luận: điều kiện để toàn cầu hóa làm giàu văn hóa.
model_paragraphs: Globalisation has brought cultures into closer contact than ever before, through trade, travel and digital media. While some people fear that this process is eroding local identities, others believe it allows cultures to learn from and enrich one another. In my view, both effects are real, and which one dominates depends largely on whether communities retain control over their own traditions.

Those who see globalisation as a threat point to the spread of a small number of global brands, entertainment industries and languages. In many cities, the same fast-food chains, clothing shops and films can be found everywhere, and young people may grow up more familiar with foreign celebrities than with their own traditions. Minority languages are particularly vulnerable, as parents often encourage their children to speak the language that offers the best economic opportunities.

On the other hand, globalisation has also created new opportunities for local cultures. Traditional music, food and crafts can now reach audiences around the world, providing income that allows artisans to continue their work. Contact with other cultures has always been a source of creativity, and many traditions that communities regard as their own were shaped by earlier exchanges. Digital technology, too, has helped some minority languages to find new speakers through online courses and social media.

Much as I recognise the risks, I believe that globalisation enriches cultures when exchange takes place on fair terms. Where communities decide how their heritage is shared and who benefits from it, contact with the wider world tends to strengthen rather than weaken their identity.

In conclusion, globalisation can both threaten and enrich local cultures. Its overall effect depends less on the amount of contact between cultures than on whether local communities have a meaningful voice in shaping that contact.

speaking.title: Culture and traditions – full test review
speaking.instruction_vi: Ôn trọn vẹn cả 3 part theo đúng thời gian thi: Part 1 (4–5 phút), Part 2 (1 phút chuẩn bị, 2 phút nói), Part 3 (4–5 phút).
speaking.focus: Chuyển mạch tự nhiên giữa 3 part: Part 1 ngắn gọn có chi tiết, Part 2 có cấu trúc, Part 3 có lập luận và nhượng bộ (much as, while).
part1: What is the most important festival in your country?
Do you enjoy trying food from other cultures?
Is there a traditional craft in your hometown?
Have you ever learned a traditional song or dance?
speaking.part2: Describe a tradition from your culture that you think should be preserved. You should say what the tradition is, how it is practised, who takes part in it, and explain why you think it should be preserved.
part3: Should governments spend money on preserving traditions that few people still follow?
How can young people be encouraged to take an interest in their own culture?
speaking.model_answer: A tradition I think really deserves to be preserved is the custom of worshipping ancestors at home, which is still practised by most families in Vietnam. Almost every house has a small altar with photographs of family members who have passed away, and on important days – the anniversary of someone's death, Lunar New Year, or the first and fifteenth day of each lunar month – the family lights incense and offers food, fruit and flowers. Usually the eldest members of the family lead the ceremony, but everyone takes part, including young children, who are taught to bow and say a few words to their grandparents' photographs. What I value about it is not so much the religious side, but the way it connects generations. On death anniversaries, relatives who live far away come home, and over the meal the older people tell stories about the person being remembered, so children learn their family history in a very natural way. Much as I understand that modern life is busy and many young people move to cities, I think it would be a real loss if this tradition disappeared, because it's one of the few occasions that reminds us where we come from and keeps the whole family in touch.
extensions: Lập trường cân bằng → nguy cơ đồng nhất hóa → cơ hội quảng bá văn hóa → điều kiện: cộng đồng kiểm soát.
Should governments spend money on preserving traditions that few people still follow?
Đồng ý có chọn lọc → giá trị bản sắc, không thể khôi phục khi mất → ưu tiên ghi chép và tạo bối cảnh mới.
How can young people be encouraged to take an interest in their own culture?
Ba cách: trường học trải nghiệm, kết hợp với thiết kế hiện đại/mạng xã hội, gia đình kể chuyện → ví dụ.

Có điều kiện → xin phép, ghi công, chia sẻ lợi ích → ví dụ thời trang → rủi ro thương mại hóa.

coaching.core: Diễn đạt sự đa dạng văn hóa bằng lập luận có điều kiện
terms: balanced evaluations with a clear position
coaching.example: Global media may broaden cultural exposure while also increasing commercial pressure on local creative work; both outcomes can coexist.
coaching.trap: Sử dụng từ tuyệt đối like always, never, everyone mà không có bằng chứng.
coaching.reading_focus: Global multiple choice and nuanced attitude questions

deep.grammar: 'While global media may...' là cấu trúc nhượng bộ, không có nghĩa hai ý có cùng trọng lượng. 'It would be simplistic to argue that...' giúp chỉ ra cách nhìn quá tuyệt đối, nhưng chỉ nên dùng khi tiếp theo có giải thích cụ thể. Chọn collocation 'cultural heritage', 'intergenerational transmission', 'local participation' phù hợp ngữ cảnh.
deep.reading: Global multiple-choice hỏi toàn bộ lập luận, không phải một ví dụ ở đoạn đầu. Đọc phần chuyển ý however, nevertheless và kết luận để xác định quan điểm tổng. Nếu tác giả cân nhắc cả hai mặt, đáp án khẳng định tác giả hoàn toàn phản đối toàn cầu hóa có thể quá cực đoan.
deep.listening: Đối với bài thảo luận văn hóa, phân biệt ý kiến từng diễn giả: speaker A lo thương mại hóa, speaker B nhấn mạnh tiếp cận quốc tế. Trong matching, tên riêng thường bị lặp lại giữa nhiều câu; cần hiểu nội dung quan điểm và lần chỉnh sửa cuối cùng.
deep.writing: Discuss both views + opinion: kể rõ hai lập trường trước khi phân tích quan điểm của mình. Band cao cần tránh cực đoan kiểu 'all local cultures disappear'. Có thể lập luận rằng chuẩn hóa thương mại tồn tại cùng với thích nghi địa phương, rồi giải thích điều kiện để nghệ sĩ và cộng đồng hưởng lợi.
